title: Pricing Services
summary: Add up what it takes → Test a price → Fair to both
subtitle: Charge a price that pays your costs, your time, and your future.

blocks.text: Pricing a service is harder than pricing a product, because your main ingredient is your own time. Many new owners guess at a number that feels polite, then wonder why they are worn out and still behind on bills. This lesson shows you how to build a price from real numbers and quote it honestly under Canadian rules.
Stop guessing, and build a price you can defend.
blocks.detail: A short calculation shows the hourly rate your business needs, so you can quote with confidence instead of worry.
blocks.extra: Section 03 walks through the calculation with a simple example.

blocks.text: A price has to cover three things at once. First, your business costs, such as tools, software, insurance and travel. Second, your own pay, which is why you started. Third, the time you cannot bill, like emails, quotes and the cleanup after a job.
Beginners often copy a competitor’s price or reuse the hourly wage from their old job. Neither one pays for the costs of running a business, your own taxes or the unpaid hours around every paid hour.
A good price is also fair to the customer. It is easy to understand, matches the value of the work and holds no nasty surprises when the final bill arrives.

sections.title: Three ways to set a price

blocks.text: Method 1: Start from your hourly rate

Start with the pay you want before tax, and add your yearly business costs. Then divide that total by the hours you can bill in a year. Most people bill far fewer hours than they work, because marketing, paperwork and travel take time too.

Say you want $60,000 before tax, and your costs are $9,000. You need $69,000 in sales. If you can bill about 1,000 hours a year, your rate is $69 an hour. At 1,500 billable hours, the same goal needs only $46 an hour, but that is hard for a one-person business to reach.

Count the time off you won’t be paid for. No one pays a self-employed person for holidays or sick days. If you take six weeks off a year and bill about 22 hours in each of the other 46 weeks, that is roughly 1,000 billable hours. Your $60,000 is also before tax: as a sole proprietor you pay income tax and both halves of CPP out of it.

items.title: Hourly rate
list: How it works: Your rate multiplied by the hours that a job takes
Best for: Work where the time is hard to predict

items.title: Fixed price
list: How it works: One price for a clearly described job
Best for: Work that you can scope in advance

items.title: Packages or value pricing
list: How it works: A set price based on the result for the customer
Best for: Work where the result matters more than the hours

blocks.text: Fixed prices reward your speed. When you quote a fixed price, you keep the gain as you get faster. Describe the job in writing first, including what is not included, so a small job does not slowly grow into a much bigger one.

items.title: “Being the cheapest is the safest way to win clients.”
items.text: A rock-bottom price draws customers who care only about price, and it leaves you no room for mistakes. Many buyers also read a price that low as a sign of weak quality.

blocks.text: Quote honestly, including fees and tax

The Competition Act bans price claims that mislead in a way that matters. Since June 23, 2022, advertising a price that leaves out a fixed fee everyone must pay counts as misleading. This is called drip pricing. The only exception is a charge the government sets, such as sales tax.

A required fee belongs in the price you quote. If every customer must pay a $15 call-out fee, include it in the price you advertise. In 2024, Sirius XM agreed to pay a $3.3 million penalty to settle concerns that a required fee raised its advertised monthly price by 10% to 20%.

If you are registered for GST/HST, add the tax on top of your fee and show it on its own line. Tell the client when you quote, so a $1,000 job in Ontario does not turn into $1,130 at the last minute. A short written quote also protects you if a disagreement comes up.

Put it in writing. A written quote should list what the job includes, the total price, the tax, your payment terms and how long the quote is good for. Ask for a deposit on larger jobs, so you are not paying for materials out of your own pocket.
The Red Toolbox
paragraphs: Hamid Rahimi was a handyman in Regina. He carried everything in a rusty red toolbox his uncle had given him. His goal was to quit his evening warehouse shift, which meant earning enough from repairs alone to cover his rent.
He charged $25 an hour, because that was what he earned at the warehouse. Clients loved him, and his calendar filled up within weeks. Yet at the end of the month, the numbers looked wrong.

Hamid sat at his kitchen table and added things up. He took off fuel, tools and insurance. Then he counted the hours he spent driving, quoting and answering messages. After costs, he was making about $9 an hour. He felt a flash of embarrassment, then a bigger flash of clarity.

Now he had a choice. He could keep the low price, keep every client and stay tired. Or he could work out a rate that would let him quit the warehouse, and risk losing some of them. He used the calculation from this lesson and landed on $55 an hour, plus a $15 call-out fee that he now built into every quote. He emailed his clients the new rates with a short, polite note.
He braced for the worst. Two of his eleven clients left. One of the others wrote back, “Finally. I was worried you couldn’t stay in business at that price.”

Within three months, Hamid worked fewer hours and earned more than before. He handed in his notice at the warehouse in the spring. The rusty red toolbox still rides in his truck, because he says it earned its place.

blocks.text: A fair price is a kindness to your clients and to yourself.
blocks.detail: When your price covers your real costs, you can do careful work, stay in business and keep serving the people who value you.
blocks.extra: Section 05 shows how to put your new price into practice.

items.title: Write down your income goal.
items.text: Use the amount you want before tax.

items.title: Add your yearly business costs.
items.text: Include tools, software, insurance, phone, travel, and advertising.

items.title: Estimate your billable hours.
items.text: Be honest about time off and the unpaid hours that come with every job.

items.title: Divide to find your rate.
items.text: Test it against what similar local businesses charge.

items.title: Quote in writing.
items.text: Include every required fee, show tax on its own line and say how long the quote is good for.

items.title: Review every six months.
items.text: Costs change and your skills grow, so your price should move too.

blocks.text: Sales tax on services, once you are registered

items.title: Alberta
items.text: 5% GST

items.title: British Columbia
items.text: 5% GST (PST applies only to certain services)

items.title: Saskatchewan
items.text: 5% GST (PST applies only to certain services)

items.title: Manitoba
items.text: 5% GST (RST applies only to certain services)

items.title: Ontario
items.text: 13% HST

items.title: Quebec
items.text: 5% GST plus 9.975% QST

items.title: Atlantic provinces
items.text: HST of 14% in Nova Scotia and 15% elsewhere

blocks.text: Rates and exemptions change, so confirm them before you file. If you are not registered yet, you do not charge tax until your taxable sales pass $30,000 over four calendar quarters, or in a single quarter.

items.title: “I should raise my price only when I lose my best clients.”
items.text: A small, regular increase is easier on everyone. Give clients notice, explain what changed, and think about keeping a loyal client’s old rate for a few months as a thank-you.

blocks.text: Insider tip: When you raise your price, send a short, warm message with the new rate, the start date and a line of thanks. A fair price needs no apology.
Quick Check

items.title: What three things must a service price cover?
items.detail: Your costs, your own pay, and the time you cannot bill.

items.title: Where does a mandatory $15 call-out fee belong?
items.text: since drip pricing is not allowed.

items.title: Can you add sales tax after the advertised price?
items.text: because government-imposed tax is the exception.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: You want $60,000 before tax and have $9,000 of costs. About how much must you bill? A. $60,000 · B. $69,000 · C. $51,000
items.text: Your sales must cover both your pay and your business costs.

items.title: Which price is the safest to advertise? A. A price that leaves out a mandatory fee · B. The total price including all mandatory fixed fees, before tax · C. A price that changes at checkout
items.text: Mandatory fixed fees belong in the price. Government tax is the main exception.

items.title: Why does a written quote help? A. It protects both you and the client by recording the scope and price · B. It lets you change the price later · C. It is required for every job
items.text: A written quote prevents misunderstandings about the work and the cost.

items.title: In one sentence, say what you will change about the way you quote prices.
items.text: I will build my rate from my real costs and put every fee in the written quote.

blocks.text: Build your price from real numbers, include every mandatory fee, show tax separately, and put the quote in writing.

items.title: Billable hours
items.text: The hours you can charge a client for.

items.title: Overhead
items.text: The ongoing costs of running your business.

items.title: Fixed price
items.text: One agreed price for a clearly described job.

items.title: Value pricing
items.text: A price based on the result for the customer, not the hours.

items.title: Drip pricing
items.text: Advertising a price that leaves out fees everyone must pay.

items.title: Quote
items.text: A written price for a defined piece of work.
